nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; African American novelist, essayist and critic of jazz and American culture
literary_identity: Novelist and essayist; the author of Invisible Man (1952), the most honoured American novel of the post-war decades, and of two collections of essays on literature, music and American identity.
biography: Ralph Waldo Ellison was born in Oklahoma City on 1 March 1913 and named after Ralph Waldo Emerson. He studied music at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama from 1933, left for New York in 1936, and there met Langston Hughes and Richard Wright, who encouraged him to write reviews and stories; he worked for the Federal Writers' Project and served in the merchant marine during the Second World War. Invisible Man, begun in 1945 and published by Random House in 1952, won the National Book Award in 1953. He held a fellowship at the American Academy in Rome in the mid-1950s, published the essays of Shadow and Act in 1964, taught at Bard, Rutgers and Yale, and held the Albert Schweitzer Chair in the Humanities at New York University from 1970 to 1979. He received the National Medal of Arts in 1985 and published a second collection, Going to the Territory, in 1986. He worked for some forty years on a second novel that he never finished. He died of pancreatic cancer in New York on 16 April 1994; his literary executor John F. Callahan edited his essays (1995), stories (1996) and the novel Juneteenth (1999) from his papers.
literary_profile: Ralph Ellison's reputation rests on one finished novel and two books of essays: Invisible Man fused the African American folk and blues tradition with the techniques of modernist fiction, and the essays argued that Black American culture is central to, not separate from, American culture as a whole.
stylistic_characteristics: A densely allusive, comic and lyrical prose that shifts between registers, from sermon, folk tale and blues to surrealist nightmare; a first-person narrator who reflects on his own telling; essays that move from personal reminiscence to cultural argument, often through jazz.
intellectual_concerns: Race and visibility in American democracy; identity as improvisation; the folk and vernacular sources of art; jazz and the blues as models of discipline and freedom; the American nation as a mixed, unfinished culture.
historical_significance: Ellison stands with Richard Wright and James Baldwin among the defining African American writers of the mid-twentieth century; Invisible Man was voted the most important American novel since the Second World War in a 1965 Book Week poll, and his essays shaped later arguments about the relation between Black culture and American identity.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth year: Wikipedia and the New World Encyclopedia give 1 March 1913; the Gale entries reproduced by Encyclopedia.com give 1914, the year found in many older references. 1913 is recorded here.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete. Recorded as works: Invisible Man (1952), Shadow and Act (1964), Going to the Territory (1986), The Collected Essays of Ralph Ellison (1995, posthumous), Flying Home and Other Stories (1996, posthumous) and Juneteenth (1999, posthumous). Also recorded (installment 10, wave 04): Trading Twelves: The Selected Letters of Ralph Ellison and Albert Murray (2000, posthumous for Ellison), with Albert Murray as co-author and co-editor. Not individually recorded: uncollected periodical pieces, including the excerpts from the unfinished second novel published in magazines between 1960 and 1977, are not individually recorded. Outside the period: Living with Music (2002), Three Days Before the Shooting... (2010) and The Selected Letters (2019). Checked against Wikipedia, Encyclopedia.com (Gale) and the New World Encyclopedia.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; British poet, novelist, jazz critic and university librarian
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and librarian; the most widely read English poet of the post-war decades and the central poet of the Movement of the 1950s.
biography: Philip Arthur Larkin was born in Coventry on 9 August 1922 and read English at St John's College, Oxford, where he began a lifelong friendship with Kingsley Amis. He became a librarian, first at Wellington in Shropshire, then as assistant librarian at University College, Leicester, from 1946, sub-librarian at Queen's University, Belfast, from 1950, and from March 1955 Librarian of the University of Hull, the post he held for the rest of his life. His first book of poems, The North Ship (1945), was followed by two novels, Jill (1946) and A Girl in Winter (1947). After a privately printed pamphlet, XX Poems (1951), The Less Deceived (1955) made his reputation, and The Whitsun Weddings (1964) and High Windows (1974) confirmed him as the leading English poet of his generation. He reviewed jazz records for the Daily Telegraph, edited The Oxford Book of Twentieth-Century English Verse (1973) and chaired the Booker Prize judges in 1977. He died of cancer in Hull on 2 December 1985. His Collected Poems (1988), Selected Letters (1992) and Andrew Motion's biography (1993) transformed his posthumous reputation.
literary_profile: Larkin's reputation rests on three mature collections of formally exact, colloquial and ironic poems about ordinary lives, love, ageing and death, together with two early novels, jazz criticism and a small body of essays.
stylistic_characteristics: Traditional stanzas and rhyme handled with conversational ease; plain, precise diction that rises in closing lines to lyrical or visionary images; irony, self-deprecation and bleak comedy; the persona of an unillusioned provincial observer.
intellectual_concerns: Mortality and the fear of death; the gap between expectation and experience; love, marriage and solitude; time and ageing; English towns, landscape and customs; the decline of religious belief and what might replace it.
historical_significance: Larkin is widely regarded as the foremost English poet of the second half of the twentieth century. His rejection of modernist difficulty in favour of a tradition descending from Thomas Hardy shaped the Movement and much later British poetry, while the posthumous letters and biography opened a lasting debate about his views on race and women.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete. Recorded as works: Jill (1946), A Girl in Winter (1947), XX Poems (1951), The Less Deceived (1955), The Whitsun Weddings (1964), All What Jazz (1970), The Oxford Book of Twentieth-Century English Verse (1973, editor), High Windows (1974), Aubade (1977), Required Writing (1983), Collected Poems (1988, posthumous) and Selected Letters of Philip Larkin, 1940-1985 (1992, posthumous). Not recorded: The Fantasy Poets No. 21 (Fantasy Press, 1954), a pamphlet whose contents have not been verified; uncollected reviews, introductions and broadcasts. Outside the period: The North Ship (1945), which belongs to the 1901-1945 window but is not yet in the database; Trouble at Willow Gables and Other Fictions (2002), Letters to Monica (2010) and The Complete Poems (2012). Checked against Wikipedia (via Wikiwand), EBSCO Research Starters, the New World Encyclopedia and the Sogang University Larkin page.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; African American playwright, essayist and civil rights activist
literary_identity: Playwright and activist; author of A Raisin in the Sun (1959), the first play by an African American woman to be produced on Broadway.
biography: Lorraine Vivian Hansberry was born in Chicago on 19 May 1930, the youngest child of a prominent African American family. When her father bought a house in the white neighbourhood of Woodlawn, the family faced a hostile reception and a legal battle over racially restrictive covenants that reached the United States Supreme Court, an experience that later shaped A Raisin in the Sun. She studied at the University of Wisconsin from 1948, left in 1950 for New York, and worked as a staff writer and then associate editor on Paul Robeson's newspaper Freedom (1951-53); in 1952 she represented Robeson at a peace congress in Montevideo. She married the songwriter and producer Robert Nemiroff in 1953; they divorced in 1964, though he remained her collaborator and literary executor. A Raisin in the Sun opened on Broadway in March 1959 and won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award. Her second play, The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window, opened in 1964. She was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 1963 and died in New York on 12 January 1965, aged thirty-four. Nemiroff later adapted To Be Young, Gifted and Black (1969) from her writings and completed and published her last plays.
literary_profile: Hansberry's few finished plays brought working-class African American family life to the centre of the American stage and joined it to a wider politics of civil rights, anti-colonialism, feminism and intellectual commitment.
stylistic_characteristics: Realist family drama with naturalistic, humorous dialogue that carries political argument; vivid, many-sided characters; symbolic objects and gestures; in the later plays a move towards the drama of ideas and fable.
intellectual_concerns: Housing segregation and racial discrimination; the American Dream and its costs; the dignity of working-class Black families; African independence and colonialism; the responsibility of intellectuals to commit themselves; women's independence.
historical_significance: A Raisin in the Sun is ranked among the classics of American drama and opened Broadway to Black playwrights, directors and audiences; Hansberry's essays, letters and late plays have made her an important figure in the histories of the civil rights movement, Black feminism and lesbian writing.
biographical_uncertainty: Her letters to the lesbian magazine The Ladder in the late 1950s were published anonymously and attributed to her later; the AmericanLiterature.com profile reports them, and the attribution is widely accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete for plays and books. Recorded as works: A Raisin in the Sun (1959), The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window (staged 1964, published 1965), The Movement: Documentary of a Struggle for Equality (1964), To Be Young, Gifted and Black (1969, adapted by Robert Nemiroff), Les Blancs (staged 1970, completed by Nemiroff), The Drinking Gourd (written 1960) and What Use Are Flowers? (both published posthumously in 1972). Not individually recorded: her journalism for Freedom (1951-55); essays and speeches such as 'On Summer' and 'The Negro Writer and His Roots'; her screenplay for the 1961 film of A Raisin in the Sun; letters published anonymously in The Ladder in the late 1950s; unfinished works. Checked against Britannica, Gale (via Encyclopedia.com) and other references listed with each record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; African American novelist, essayist, biographer and jazz critic
literary_identity: Novelist, essayist and jazz critic; theorist of the blues as the basis of American culture and author of the four Scooter novels.
biography: Albert Lee Murray was born in Nokomis, Alabama, on 12 May 1916 and was adopted and raised in Magazine Point, on the outskirts of Mobile. He graduated from Tuskegee Institute in 1939, taught there, and served in the Army Air Forces during the Second World War. He took an MA at New York University in 1948 and studied at the Sorbonne in 1950, then returned to active duty in 1951 and retired from the US Air Force as a major in 1962. He settled in Harlem and published essays in magazines before collecting them as The Omni-Americans (1970), which was followed by a travel memoir, critical lectures, four novels about a boy called Scooter and several books on jazz, including the as-told-to autobiography of Count Basie. He taught at Barnard College in 1981-83 and held visiting posts elsewhere; his ideas influenced the critic Stanley Crouch and the trumpeter Wynton Marsalis, with whom he co-founded the programme that became Jazz at Lincoln Center in the 1980s. The National Book Critics Circle gave him its lifetime achievement award in 1996. He died in Harlem on 18 August 2013, aged ninety-seven.
literary_profile: Murray's essays, fiction and jazz writing argue that American culture is fundamentally a blend of Black and white traditions and that the blues and jazz provide a model of heroic improvisation in the face of adversity.
stylistic_characteristics: Densely allusive, rhythmic prose modelled on jazz and blues forms; first-person narration rich in vernacular storytelling; essays that mix literary, anthropological and musical analysis with polemic.
intellectual_concerns: The blues as an art of confronting adversity; the hybrid, 'Omni-American' character of national culture; heroism and improvisation; critique of social-science and protest images of Black life; Southern memory and education.
historical_significance: Murray was a central voice in the long argument against protest fiction and Black separatism, and his writing on the blues and jazz shaped the institutional revival of jazz in the United States from the 1980s onwards.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete. Recorded as works: The Omni-Americans (1970), South to a Very Old Place (1971), The Hero and the Blues (1973), Train Whistle Guitar (1974), Stomping the Blues (1976), Good Morning Blues: The Autobiography of Count Basie (1985, as-told-to collaborator), The Spyglass Tree (1991), The Seven League Boots (1996), The Blue Devils of Nada (1996) and Trading Twelves (2000, co-edited correspondence with Ralph Ellison, recorded under Ellison with Murray as co-author). Unresolved: Reflections on Logic, Politics, and Reality: A Challenge to the Sacred Consensus of Contemporary American Thinking (Braimanna, 1989) appears in the Gale Contemporary Literary Criticism bibliography and in the Alabama Authors database, but its attribution to this Albert Murray has not been independently confirmed, so it has no work record. Not individually recorded: uncollected magazine essays and reviews. Outside the period: Conjugations and Reiterations (2001), From the Briarpatch File (2001), Murray Talks Music (2016) and the Library of America collected editions.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Nigerian; Yoruba (Egba) novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: Novelist and storyteller whose The Palm-Wine Drinkard (1952) was the first Nigerian book to win international fame; author of eleven books (1952-1990) that rework Yoruba folktales as quest romances in an idiosyncratic West African English.
biography: Amos Olatubosun Tutuola was born on 20 June 1920 at or near Abeokuta, in the Egba country of Yorubaland, then under British rule; Wikipedia names the village of Wasinmi, Gale's Contemporary Black Biography the Ipose-Ake quarter of Abeokuta. His parents, Charles and Esther Tutuola, were Yoruba Christian cocoa farmers. He had about six years of schooling, including the Salvation Army primary school and the Anglican Central School in Abeokuta, which ended when his father died in 1939. He then trained as a smith and worked as a blacksmith (some accounts say coppersmith) for the Royal Air Force in Nigeria during the Second World War (1942-45 in Wikipedia, 1943-45 in the Gale entries). After failing to set up his own smithy, he became a messenger in the Department of Labour in Lagos in 1948, having married Victoria Alake in 1947. In the idle hours of that job he began writing English versions of Yoruba tales. His first manuscript, The Wild Hunter in the Bush of the Ghosts, was sent to the London photographic publisher Focal Press in the late 1940s and not printed until 1982. The Palm-Wine Drinkard, passed to Faber and Faber by the United Society for Christian Literature, appeared in London in 1952 and New York in 1953. From 1956 he worked as a storekeeper for the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in Ibadan. He was a founding member of the Mbari Club, a visiting research fellow at the University of Ife in 1979 and an associate of the International Writing Program at the University of Iowa in 1983. In retirement he lived between Ibadan and Ago-Odo. He died at Ibadan on 8 June 1997, of hypertension and diabetes. His papers are held by the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin.
literary_profile: Tutuola's books retell and recombine Yoruba folktales as long episodic quests: a naive, idle or headstrong hero or heroine travels into the bush of spirits, survives monsters and captivities by cunning, magic or a protector's help, and comes home changed. Eight novels, an early manuscript published late (Contemporary Black Biography counts nine 'epic novels' in all), a school collection of traditional tales and a final book of stories make up the published output. He also wrote short stories for periodicals and anthologies and unpublished plays reworking the same material.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person oral narration in the early books (Simbi, 1955, is the first in the third person), in an English shaped by Yoruba syntax and idiom, with coinages, irregular grammar and spelling, and objects of modern life set in a world of spirits. Episodes are loosely linked, and Tutuola himself declined to call his books novels. The register changes in Yoruba Folktales (1986), written for schools in standard English.
intellectual_concerns: Journeys to the land of the dead and the bush of ghosts; death, famine and poverty, including poverty inherited and apparently permanent; greed, betrayal and trickery; the testing and education of a weak or disobedient protagonist; parents who fail or are lost; the preservation and performance of Yoruba oral tradition.
historical_significance: Tutuola was the first Nigerian writer to achieve international recognition. The reception of The Palm-Wine Drinkard became a test case for African writing in English: acclaim in Britain and the United States, hostility among educated Nigerians who thought its language and spirits shamed the country on the eve of independence, and later reassessment of his work as a creative transmission of oral tradition into print. The taxonomy of this database dates African literature in English from his first book.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete. All eleven books are recorded as works: The Palm-Wine Drinkard (1952), My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (1954), Simbi and the Satyr of the Dark Jungle (1955), The Brave African Huntress (1958), Feather Woman of the Jungle (1962), Ajaiyi and His Inherited Poverty (1967), The Witch-Herbalist of the Remote Town (1981), The Wild Hunter in the Bush of the Ghosts (written in the late 1940s, published 1982), Yoruba Folktales (1986), Pauper, Brawler and Slanderer (1987) and The Village Witch Doctor and Other Stories (1990). The list agrees across Wikipedia, Britannica (which omits The Wild Hunter), Gale's Contemporary Black Biography and ISFDB. Not recorded separately: short stories that ISFDB lists with years of first appearance in periodicals and anthologies. They are 'The Strange Fellows' Palm-Wine Tapster' and 'Tort and the Dancing Market-Women' (1952), 'My First Wedding Day in the Bush of Ghosts' (1954), 'The Elephant Woman' (1956; revised in Yoruba Folktales), 'Ajaiyi and the Witch Doctor' (1959), 'Ajantala, the Noxious Guest' and 'Don't Pay Bad for Bad' (1960), 'The Duckling Brothers and Their Disobedient Sister' (1961), 'The Town of Famine' (1962, from Feather Woman of the Jungle), 'Remember the Day After Tomorrow' (1969), 'Akanke and the Jealous Pawnbroker' (1974) and 'Tort's Bitter Marriage' (1984). Four of them were collected in The Village Witch Doctor; their first venues and texts were not consulted. Also not recorded: the unpublished plays Ajaiyi and the Witch Doctor, The Pupils of the Eyes and The Sword of Vengeance, known from Chris Dunton's study of the manuscripts at the Harry Ransom Center; a 1958 drama titled The Palm-Wine Drinkard listed by Gale's Contemporary Literary Criticism and not identified further; the radio tale 'Dola with her Colanut Tree' (BBC West Africa Service, 1954); and the posthumous collection Don't Pay Bad for Bad (2012), outside the period. Unresolved dates: Simbi (1955; 1956 in two Gale entries) and The Witch-Herbalist (1981; 1980 in the Encyclopedia of World Biography).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Barbadian; Caribbean (West Indian) novelist, essayist and poet writing in English, in England from 1950 and later based again in Barbados
literary_identity: Barbadian novelist and essayist whose six novels (1953-1972) follow colonial Caribbean society from the plantation village to migration, independence and the slave-trading voyages of its origins, and whose The Pleasures of Exile (1960) reread The Tempest from Caliban's side.
biography: George William Lamming was born on 8 June 1927 in Carrington Village, a former plantation settlement near Bridgetown, Barbados, of mixed African and English parentage, and was raised chiefly by his mother, Loretta Devonish. A scholarship took him from Roebuck Boys' School to Combermere School, where Frank Collymore, founder and editor of the magazine Bim, encouraged his writing; Bim published his early poems and prose. From 1946 to 1950 he taught at El Colegio de Venezuela, a boarding school for boys in Port of Spain, Trinidad. In 1950 he sailed to England on the same boat as Samuel Selvon, worked briefly in a factory, and from 1951 broadcast for the BBC's Colonial Service; its Caribbean Voices programme aired his poems and short prose. In the Castle of My Skin (1953) won a Somerset Maugham Award (1957), and fellowships from the Kenyon Review (1954) and the Guggenheim Foundation (1954 or 1955; sources differ) made him a professional writer. He travelled to the United States in 1955, the West Indies in 1956 and West Africa in 1958, and by 1960 had published four novels and The Pleasures of Exile. In the 1960s he published no novel: he co-edited the Barbados and Guyana independence issues of New World Quarterly (1965, 1967), wrote a television documentary script about the Freedom Riders, held a Canada Council fellowship (1962) and was writer-in-residence at the University of the West Indies, Mona, Jamaica (1967-68). Water with Berries (1971) and Natives of My Person (1972) were his last novels. He returned to Barbados in the late 1970s and held visiting posts at the universities of Texas at Austin, Pennsylvania and Connecticut, at Brown, Cornell and Duke, and lectured in Denmark, Tanzania and Australia. He was made a Companion of Honour of Barbados (1987), received the Langston Hughes Medal of the City University of New York (1998) and was awarded the Order of the Caribbean Community (2008). He died in Bridgetown on 4 June 2022.
literary_profile: Lamming's fiction follows the stages of Caribbean history and of his own life: a Barbadian village at the end of the plantation order (In the Castle of My Skin, 1953); the voyage to England and the migrants' disillusion there (The Emigrants, 1954); the imagined island of San Cristobal on the eve of independence and just after it (Of Age and Innocence, 1958; Season of Adventure, 1960); West Indian artists in London as Caliban's heirs (Water with Berries, 1971); and an early colonial voyage of slavers and settlers (Natives of My Person, 1972). He described his novels as parts of one book that need not be read in order. The Pleasures of Exile (1960) mixes autobiography and criticism, and later volumes of essays, addresses and interviews (1992, 1995) carry his concerns with politics, culture and the education of the Caribbean intellectual. His poems and stories appeared in Bim, on the BBC and in anthologies but were never collected.
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, lyrical and often difficult prose with shifting points of view: villagers or emigrants speak in turn as in a play, dreams and reveries interrupt the narrative, an intrusive 'Author's Note' breaks into Season of Adventure, and Natives of My Person imitates early maritime prose. Gerald Moore, in Contemporary Novelists, found a complexity of form and texture that only Wilson Harris matched among West Indian novelists; Novels for Students points to the modernist devices of shifting perspective and unreliable narration in the first novel.
intellectual_concerns: Colonialism and its psychological legacy, which he called 'a terror of the mind'; land, labour and the end of the plantation village; colonial education; migration and the discovery of a West Indian identity in England; independence and the failures of nationalist leaders; the Caribbean's African inheritance and women's experience, both new in Season of Adventure; Caliban and Prospero as figures of the colonised and the coloniser; slavery, the Middle Passage and the founding violence of colonial society.
historical_significance: Lamming is a founding figure of modern Caribbean writing in English. In the Castle of My Skin, praised by Richard Wright and Jean-Paul Sartre and read by Ngugi wa Thiong'o as one of the great political novels of colonial literature, remains the most cited of his books; The Emigrants is among the first novels of Caribbean migration to Britain; and his rereading of Caliban in The Pleasures of Exile became, in the words of the Encyclopedia of African-American Culture and History, a representative symbol of anticolonial resistance and of postcolonial theory. Novels for Students ranks him with V. S. Naipaul and Derek Walcott among the most important figures of Anglophone Caribbean literature.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete for books. All six novels and three books of essays are recorded as works: In the Castle of My Skin (1953), The Emigrants (1954), Of Age and Innocence (1958), Season of Adventure (1960), The Pleasures of Exile (1960), Water with Berries (1971), Natives of My Person (1972), Conversations: Essays, Addresses and Interviews 1953-1990 (1992) and Coming, Coming Home: Conversations II (1995). Not recorded as works, because their contents were not examined: the uncollected stories 'David's Walk' (Life and Letters, November 1948), 'Of Thorns and Thistles' and 'A Wedding in Spring' (in Andrew Salkey's West Indian Stories, 1960), 'Birds of a Feather' (in Salkey's Stories from the Caribbean, 1965) and 'Birthday Weather' (in G. R. Coulthard's Caribbean Literature, 1966); his poems in Bim, on Caribbean Voices and in anthologies, which no source consulted enumerates; the anthologies he edited, Cannon Shot and Glass Beads: Modern Black Writing (Pan, 1974) and On the Canvas of the World (Trinidad and Tobago Institute of the West Indies, 1999); Influencia del Africa en las literaturas antillanas (with Henry Bangou and Rene Depestre, Montevideo, 1972) and The Most Important People (with Kathleen Drayton, Bridgetown, 1981), both listed only in Contemporary Novelists; the Barbados and Guyana independence issues of New World Quarterly that he co-edited (1965, 1967); a television documentary script on the Freedom Riders (Contemporary Black Biography); and his direction of the play Meet Me at Golden Hill (Barbados, 1974). Outside the period: The Sovereignty of the Imagination: Conversations III (2009) and Caribbean Reasonings: The George Lamming Reader (ed. Anthony Bogues, 2010). Checked against Wikipedia's list of published works, the bibliography in Contemporary Novelists, the selected writings in Contemporary Black Biography and Britannica. Discrepancies: the date of Natives of My Person (1972 in Wikipedia and the Gale entries, 1971 in Britannica, and the Writers Directory entry on Encyclopedia.com gives Natives 1971 and Water with Berries 1972); the year of the Guggenheim Fellowship (1955 in Wikipedia and Contemporary Black Biography, 1954 in Contemporary Novelists); his middle name (William in Wikipedia and Britannica, Eric in Contemporary Novelists); his household (the Gale entries call his mother unmarried, while Wikipedia records her marriage to his stepfather); and his birthplace, which Wikipedia links to Carrington in the parish of Saint Philip, while Britannica and Contemporary Black Biography place Carrington Village near Bridgetown.
